cells.tense: You hold what you know before you say it, and the holding is doing its job.
cells.ask: Close one open question today by naming the answer you already carry, and say when you'll act on it.
cells.core: Something is already settled in you, and you haven't said it yet. That's not a delay — what you know arrives before the words do, and you're letting it finish arriving. You can hold two sides of a thing without flinching away from either, which is why the pause reads as solid instead of stuck.\n\nPeople around you can feel that you won't say more than you mean, and it changes how they bring things to you. This only holds if something finally gets said. Keep the pause short and it stays strong. Let it become the whole answer and it hardens into distance. Pick one live question, put the answer out loud, and put a date on it.
cells.sheetLine: Holding what you know until it's ready to be said.
cells.verb: holding what is known before saying it

cells.tense: You will have weighed the choice so many times that the choosing never arrives.
cells.ask: Choose the option you'd defend today, say it in one sentence, and start the first step before you re-examine it.
cells.core: You're trying to know the whole shape of a decision before you take it. Every angle gets another pass, another comparison, another check that the thing is really understood — and all that examining has taken the place of moving. It feels like care. From outside it looks like the choice receding as you approach it.\n\nThe pause this names is real, but pause isn't supposed to be a residence. Fear of committing dressed as thoroughness is still fear, and it doesn't protect you — it just keeps the direction unwritten longer. What's on the other side is simpler than you're making it: decide, act, let the result inform the next move instead of your next round of weighing. Choose, say it once, take the first step.
cells.sheetLine: You're trying to know before you choose. That order doesn't exist.
cells.verb: holding what is known before saying it

cells.tense: You knew something once and have been standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.ask: Tell one person the direction you want to take, in plain words, before you feel ready to say it well.
cells.core: You're not unknowing. You're not deciding either. What you know is there — it's the saying that stopped. It stays inside, where it can't be wrong and can't be used. Meanwhile the direction goes unchosen, and that starts to look like not having one.\n\nWhat's needed isn't to force a decision. It's to let something be received. Say one true thing to one person, badly, before you've polished it — not to be told what to do, just to have it land outside you. Watch what comes back. That exchange is what feeds the part of you that picks direction, and it runs on giving and getting, not on private certainty. Say it plainly, imperfectly, to someone.
cells.sheetLine: You knew it. The saying is what stopped.
cells.verb: holding what is known before saying it

cells.tense: You are already choosing direction, and you keep describing it as just what happened.
cells.ask: Say "this is what I'm choosing" aloud about something you've been calling inevitable, before the day ends.
cells.core: Look at how you actually spend your time — what you refuse, what you let pass, what you turn toward without ceremony. That's a direction, and you're already walking it. But when you talk about it, the language slides off you: it's just what made sense, just how things went, just what was there. You are steering. You haven't worded it yet.\n\nThat gap costs you. A direction nobody owns is a direction you can't correct, defend, or hand to anyone else. Saying it plainly isn't boasting — it's just putting your name where your feet already are. Choose one thing you've treated as a given and admit you're the one picking it.
cells.sheetLine: You're choosing this already. You haven't worded it yet.
